title: Manjari 8. The Four Sampradayas
html:
Why Mahaprabhu accepted a guru; the search for Mahaprabhu's succession and the finding of Gopala-guru's record; the explanation of the Hari-nama; the Padma-purana on the four sampradayas; the Sri-sampradaya (Ramanuja, Ramananda), the Brahma-sampradaya (Madhva — Madhavendra Puri — Mahaprabhu), the "Nimanandi"; Gopala Bhatta — Srinivasa — Ramacharana Chakravarti — Ramasharana Chattaraja, the author's guru, and ten shlokas on him; the Rudra-sampradaya (Vishnusvami, Vallabha, Vitthalanatha); the Sanaka-sampradaya (Nimbaditya, Harivyasa); conclusion and date

[p. 107]

Vasanta-saurashtri.

1Bow down to Sri Krishna Chaitanya with His associates —
the limit of compassion, besides whom there is no other.

2Begging them Himself, He distributes the highest goal to the fallen;
the name "Purifier of the fallen" has now come true.

3One more consideration has arisen in my mind;
therefore I take care to write it down.

4Sri Gauranga Mahaprabhu is the son of the king of Vraja;
what need had He to accept a guru?

5If you say: the Lord follows the way of bhakti,
acting as people do in order to inspire their faith —

6if that is the reason, then why, for so small a cause,
should Gora Raya, the guru of the world, accept a guru?

7(Answer:) The Lord establishes the sanatana-dharma;
everyone knows the statement of the Padma-purana about it.1

8When the Lord is merciful to the servant of His servants,
the Antaryami and the other shaktis go about in his service.

9This Lord, Himself the source of all avataras,
who performs His pastimes with His associates whenever and however He wishes —

10would He break (the order) in practising bhakti?
Reflecting on this, I was greatly amazed.2

[p. 108]

11Then in Sri Vrindavana and Mathura
I questioned all four sampradayas.

12Three sampradayas brought me
the succession of their gurus — I saw them all.

13Not finding an account of Mahaprabhu's sampradaya,
I searched everywhere, troubled.

14Thus, after searching and searching for some days,
suddenly by the Lord's mercy I found it.

15In Sri Jiva Gosvami's kunja there is a man
of the family (of disciples) of Sri Gopala-guru Gosani —

16an old Vaishnava named Radhavallabha Dasa.
To him I told this whole story.

17He says: "Sri Gopala-guru Gosani
has already determined this — do not worry."

18Saying this, he gave me an old manuscript
and mercifully dispelled my doubts.

19An associate of Mahaprabhu is Pandita Vakreshvara;
his disciple is the excellent Sri Gopala-guru.

20The explanation of Sri Hari-nama and the determination of the sampradaya
the Mahashaya had composed and kept beforehand.

21His seat is in Nilachala, the service of Radhakanta;
it is most charming — who could describe it?3

The Explanation of Sri Hari-nama.

22In the Hari-nama there are three names:
"Hare", "Krishna", "Rama"; hear the explanation attentively.

[p. 109]

23The word "Hari" in the vocative gives "Hare";
and the word "Hara" in the vocative also gives "Hare".

24Therefore two shlokas give the meaning of the word "Hare",
and two more the meaning of the names "Krishna" and "Rama".

25In these four shlokas explaining the Hari-nama,
(Gopala-guru) gave instruction to Mahaprabhu's family.

26Thus the shlokas: "Revealing the truth of Bhagavan, whose form is concentrated consciousness and bliss, He removes ignorance and its effects; therefore He is remembered as Hari. She steals the mind of Sri Krishna, She whose nature is Krishna's delight; therefore by the word 'Hara' (vocative 'Hare') Sri Radha is glorified. The master of the sole joy of bliss, Shyama, lotus-eyed, the delight of Gokula, the son of Nanda — He is called Krishna. The embodiment of the whole essence of artfulness, the presiding deity of the pastimes, He eternally delights Radhika — therefore He is called Rama."4

27This meaning is the treasure of the devotees' lives,
or a festival for the body, or an elixir for the ears.

28The manuscript with the determination of the sampradaya that (he) had —
by good fortune I found that manuscript there.

29Finding it, I rejoiced
and copied it onto new leaves.

30Having examined Mahaprabhu's sampradaya,
I found many witnesses in Vrindavana, in Gauda and in Utkala.

[p. 110]

31In the commentary that Sri Vallabha Acharya established
he wrote of the four sampradayas.

32There too I found this shloka as proof;
I came to know firmly the statement of the Padma-purana.

33Thus in the Sri Padma-purana: "Mantras outside a sampradaya are considered fruitless. Therefore in Kali there will be four (founders of) sampradayas — the Vaishnavas Sri, Brahma, Rudra and Sanaka, who purify the earth. These four will appear in Kali as founders of sampradayas; they will become renowned from Purushottama in Utkala. The guru is one, in the Krishna mantra, a Vaishnava of a sampradaya; one who abandons him and so on falls from the highest goal."5

34First the Sri-sampradaya, then the Brahma-sampradaya,
then Rudra, then Sanaka — so the sampradayas are listed.

The Sri-sampradaya.

35By the word "Sri" Lakshmi is meant: from Her
the sampradaya has come down — so it is said for certain.

36In the beginning the Vaishnavas of this sampradaya
were called the "Sri-sampradaya".

37In time it had many branches and sub-branches;
after them Sri Ramanuja appeared.

38His name is Sri Lakshmana Acharya;
with great respect all call him Ramanuja Acharya.

[p. 111]

39He composed the Ramanuja-bhashya,
refuted jnana and karma, and established the truth of bhakti.

40Ramanuja Acharya became famous throughout the world;
by his name the sampradaya went on for some time.

41After many branches and sub-branches
Sri Ramananda Acharya became famous.

42From then on it is the Ramanandi sampradaya.
(I have) spoken briefly, fearing great prolixity.

The Brahma-sampradaya.

43"Srimat Narayana, Brahma, Narada and Vyasa; Sri Madhva, Padmanabha, Narahari, Madhava; Akshobhya, Jayatirtha, Jnanasindhu, Mahanidhi, Vidyanidhi, Rajendra, the sage Jayadharma; Purushottama, Brahmanya, the sage Vyasatirtha; Sriman Lakshmipati, Sriman Madhavendra Puri, the best (of them); then Sri Krishna Chaitanya, the wish-fulfilling tree of prema on earth, who is renowned in the world by the name Nimananda."6

44Sri Purushottama Mahashaya, dear to Nityananda —
his disciple is Sri Devakinandana Thakura.

45In the Vaishnava-vandana that he composed
he wrote of the four sampradayas;

46and in it the Madhva-sampradaya is given in the same way;
he set forth the meaning of these shlokas in Bengali.7

[p. 112]

47Everywhere, in every land, this is widespread;
look and listen, and then know it for certain.

48First comes Sri Madhvacharya, the author of the commentary;
in the Madhva-bhashya he determined the truth of bhakti.

49Down to Ishvara Puri Gosani — thus:
this is known in the world as the Madhva-sampradaya.

50When Sri Mahaprabhu appeared,
before all His other names He received the name Nimai.

51By that name, by Mahaprabhu's own will,
the "Nimanandi" sampradaya arose in due succession.8

52Formerly worship was predominantly in aishvarya;
this sweetness (madhurya) He had not given for a long time.

53Then Krishna, the Beginningless, taking the name Nimai,
bestowed the four kinds of bhakti-rasa.

54Nilambara Chakravarti, knowing the inner truth,
spoke (of this) at the name-giving ceremony.9

55Especially the unique manifestation of ujjvala-rasa:
to bestow it, (He displayed) His pastimes at the beginning of Kali.

56Accepting a lustre that surpasses pure gold,
in the midst of Navadvipa Gaurahari descended.

57May that Hari appear in the cave of everyone's heart —
He whose roar destroys the pride of the elephant of Kali.

58Sri Rupa Gosani made us experience this
in the mangalacharana of the Vidagdha-madhava.

[p. 113]

59Thus (the verse): "May the son of Shachi — Hari, radiant with a lustre more beautiful than gold, who has descended in Kali out of mercy to bestow what had not been given for a long time, the highest, radiant rasa, the wealth of devotion to Himself — ever appear in the cave of your heart."10

60As far as the ocean, whoever bears the name of Vaishnava,
on hearing "Nimanandi", everyone regards (him) as worshipful.

61Endless is His family, an abode of all virtues;
among them is one named Sri Gopala Bhatta.

62He has many disciples — they cannot be counted;
I write of one — Srinivasa Acharya Mahashaya.

63How many disciples he had I cannot say;
I write of one — Sri Ramacharana Chakravarti.

64He has a large assembly of disciples;
among them is one — Sri Ramasharana Chattaraja.

65The chief servant of Sri Acharya Thakura
is named Sri Krishnadasa Chattaraja Thakura;

66(Ramasharana) is his son, supremely serene;
his feet are my only shelter.

67He is my guru; I hope to attain his feet;
the name he gave me is my name — Manohara Dasa.11

68Near Katwa is Baganakola, his seat and home;
he lived there, having left all other homes.

[p. 114]

69What he did for me, the lowly, and how;
what compassion he had for living beings;

70how he relished sankirtana;
how talk of Krishna was revealed in him;

71his beauty, virtues, generosity, Vaishnava character —
seeing and hearing them, people marvel.

72If I wished to describe this even briefly,
it would still make a separate book.

73So I shall tell a little of how he
wondrously sent me off to Vrindavana.

74At the parting, placing his foot
on my head, he spoke these sweet words:

75"Go ahead, I shall come after;
you will certainly see me in Vrindavana."

76By his order, without hindrance, to Vrindavana
I came and obtained darshana.

77Thus I was then living at Radha-kunda;
in the second year, at night, I had a dream:

78my Prabhu came to Sri Kunda, where I lived;
springing up in awe, I offered dandavat obeisances.

79When I asked for news, he said to me:
"Have you forgotten that I told you I would come?

80'Go ahead, I shall come after' —
here I have come: see me before you."

[p. 115]

81Having seen the dream, my heart rejoiced:
I understood that the Prabhu would soon come.

82While I waited thus for some days,
suddenly the news of the Prabhu's departure came.

83Although my body (heart) is very hard,
remembering his virtues my mind was distraught.

84Some days later, thinking and thinking of that mercy,
ten shlokas came to me in this way.

85Shamelessly I write them, though I fear in my heart:
if I do not write them, it will be the offense of ingratitude.

86Thus they are: "Great one, in whom the sovereign realm of the sweetness of Gauranga, the ocean of mercy, has taken form; skilled in the work of flooding the world; whose sole refuge is Sri kirtana; whose senses and body are permeated by all those bhavas; ever the abode of my life — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? Raising hands tender as shoots, softly, softly uttering the names of Hari, eyes clouded (with tears), with the wealth of faltering voice and trembling, swiftly whirling, your body beaded with drops of sweat and tears, falling at the end of sankirtana — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? Standing for a moment stunned, then suddenly raising a loud cry, celebrating a festival of dance with gestures of sorrow and glimmers of remembrance, overcome by the excess of relishing the fragrance of the sweetness of that rasa — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? With a lustre like gold, with curling hair, with the gleam of the urdhva-pundra on your forehead, with eyes beautiful as red lotuses, with earrings swinging in your ears, with a pair of brows lovely where they meet, with a fine high nose — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? With a clear face like a blossoming lotus, with a shining row of teeth, with the sweetness of red lips — oh! — with the kanthi and the letters of the Name on your neck, a neck like a lion's, with mighty arms like an elephant's trunk — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? On your broad chest a spotless sacred thread and a charming garland falling to the waist, ever shining, wearing four fine garments, with the radiance of lotus feet — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? Dwelling by the Ganga, at the lotus feet of Gaura, the ocean of mercy, solely out of ardent desire, for bathing and darshana, daily delighting the Vaishnavas who go there with whatever they desire — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? Anointed with sandal paste from toe to crown, leaning on a cushion, immersing the good people seated around you, who have taken shelter in love for your feet, in the waves of the heavenly river of the nectar of talks about Radha and Krishna — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? By the force of the power of your blessed feet seizing me, given to lowly service, right there by my shikha, you granted me residence in your Vrindavana; what more can I say? — your heart is full of compassion for wretched people — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? You, who at every step revived (me) with your own nectar of mercy, manifesting life even in me who came (to you) — what pain did you not (remove)? Not seeing all this in you now, I have fallen into distress even here — alas, O lord of the Chattas, shall I ever see you again, O Prabhu? Whoever, with a yearning heart, every day in the morning recites this decad, which indicates the form of Sri lord of the Chattas and bears a particle of his virtues — for that noble-minded one may that very ocean, full of the nectar of mercy, soon fulfil the long-unattainable desire dwelling in his heart." Thus is completed (the poem) indicating a particle of the virtues and form of Srimad Ramasharana Chattaraja Prabhu.12

[p. 117]

The Rudra-sampradaya.

87Third is the Sri Rudra-sampradaya, renowned in the south;
the Gosanis of Gokula-dvara also trace themselves to it.

88From Sri Maharudra comes Sri Vishnusvami;
of his family I have heard from their own lips.

89Many branches and sub-branches sprang from it;
Sri Vallabhacharya became the adhikari of Nathji.

90Then the sampradaya went by the name "Vallabhi";
his son and disciple was Sri Vitthalanatha.

91From him the sampradaya is called "Vitthaleshvari".
I have spoken briefly — it cannot be told in full.13

The Sri Sanaka-sampradaya.

92First, the manifestation of Sri Narayana;
from Him, the play of Sri Hamsa in (His) form.

93His disciples are Sanaka and the others, four in number;
Narada is their disciple, of incomparable glory.

[p. 118]

94His disciple is Srinivasa Acharya Mahashaya;
Vishvacharya took shelter at his feet.

95His disciple is Purushottama Acharya, great of mind;
his disciple is Vilasacharya, renowned in the world.

96His disciple is the well-known Sri Svarupa Acharya;
Sri Madhavacharya is certainly his disciple.

97His disciple — know it — is Balabhadra Acharya;
Padmacharya is his disciple, as (all) accept.

98Sri Shyamacharya is his chief disciple;
Gopalacharya is his disciple, a treasury of virtues.

99His disciple is Kripacharya, most virtuous;
his disciple is Devacharya, devoted to his guru.

100His disciple is Sri Sundara Bhatta Mahashaya;
his disciple is Padmanabha Bhatta, the merciful.

101His disciple is Upendra Bhatta, most fortunate,
the object of love and devotion for all Vaishnavas.

102Ramachandra Bhatta is his incomparable disciple;
his disciple is Sri Vamana Bhatta, an abode of virtues.

103Sri Krishna Bhatta is his disciple,
and Padmakara Bhatta is the disciple of that one.

104His servant is Sri Shravana Bhatta;
his disciple is Sri Nimbaditya Mahashaya.

105How he came to be named Nimbaditya
I shall tell; listen attentively.

[p. 119]

106One day he invited a danda-bearing sannyasi,
with great humility and care.

107With much bustle the cooking lasted till evening;
when all was ready, the mahanta offered the bhoga.

108When they called the sannyasi, he said:
"After sunset I do not eat."

109Hurriedly (the mahanta) says: "Come, look quickly:
the sun-god is still standing above the nim tree."

110In his courtyard there was a nim tree;
above it he showed him the sun.

111Believing it, he ate;
seeing his devotion, he was very pleased.

112When he sat down, six dandas of the night had struck;
the sannyasi understood his great power.

113He showed the sun (aditya) above the nim (nimba) —
for that reason he was named Nimbaditya.14

114Sri Bhuri Bhatta is the vessel of his mercy;
Sri Madhava Bhatta remembers his feet;

115at his feet took shelter — know it — Shyama Bhatta;
Sri Gopala Bhatta, it is said, is his servant;

116Balabhadra Bhatta is his chief servant;
his servant is named Gopinatha Bhatta;

117Sri Keshava Bhatta is his disciple, great of mind;
Sri Gangala Bhatta is his disciple, wholly devoted;

[p. 120]

118Sri Keshava Kashmiri, I say, is his disciple;
the vessel of his mercy is Sri Bhatta, (I know) for certain.

119His disciple is Sri Hari-vyasa Adhikari;
he has two disciples, givers of joy to all:

120Sri Parashurama and Sri Shobhurama,
both with great bhakti, power and a wealth of virtues.

121The seat of one is at Salemabad,
the seat of the second is certainly at Budiya.

122Parashurama's disciple is Svami Sri Harivamsha,
whose virtues are praised in the assemblies of bhagavatas;

123his disciple is Sri Narayana Dasa, great of mind;
his disciple is Sri Vrindavana Dasa, most virtuous.

124Shobhurama's disciple is Sri Kanhar(?) Dasa;
his disciple is Sri Narayana Dasa;

125Sri Paramananda Dasa is his disciple:
boundless are his virtues — who can reach their end?

126His dear disciple is the Naga Sri Chatur Dasa:
by Krishna's command he settled in Vraja.

127His disciple is Svami Sri Mohana Dasa,
a maha-bhagavata, firm in faith.

128His disciple is Svami Sri Jagannatha Mahashaya;
his disciple is Sri Makhan Dasa, full of bhakti-rasa.

129In this sampradaya the branches and sub-branches are countless Vaishnavas;
all the spreading of these two branches cannot be written.

[p. 121]

130Therefore what has been written is brief;
so too the description of all the other branches.

131The Sri Sanaka-sampradaya is the fourth in number;
at first it was proclaimed as the "Sanaka-sampradaya".

132After many branches came Sri Nimbaditya:
he, a maha-bhagavata, became the mahanta.

133From then on it was called the sampradaya of Nimbaditya;
so it went on for some time.

134Gradually, some time later, Sri Hari-vyasa
became the mahanta, firm in faith in bhakti.

135From then on the sampradaya is called "Hari-vyasi".
I have spoken briefly, without going into detail.

136So (I have) pointed out the direction of the four sampradayas;
examining this, you will find all the details.

137Those whose all-in-all is Sri Rupa with his family —
for their joy this pastime is proclaimed.

138Wishing to describe this connection, the gurus and the rest,
Manohara Dasa tells the Anuraga-valli.

Thus ends, in the Srimad Anuraga-valli, the eighth manjari, called "The Determination of the Four Sampradayas".

[p. 122]

Conclusion.

139Whoever at the feet of Sri Mahaprabhu Krishna Chaitanya
offers the eight manjaris in recitation

140has pure prema for the Lord's holy feet;
he attains the associates of Chaitanya without hindrance.

141Therefore read and listen, do not be idle,
if in your heart there is a longing to see the secret.

142Making the lotus feet of Sri Guru
the ornament of my head, (I) have completed the Anuraga-valli.

143To serve those feet is my constant desire:
so Manohara Dasa speaks of his heart's wish.

Here this Anuraga-valli is completed.

144"When the samvat year counted by Rama, arrow, horse and moon had passed, in Vrindavana the 'Anuraga-vallika' was completed. In the shaka year (counted by) vasu, moon and kala, in the bright half of the month of Chaitra, at the close of the tenth lunar day, in Vrindavana the 'Anuraga-vallika' was completed." Samvat 1753. Shaka 1618.15

Notes

  1. The Padma-purana on mantras outside a sampradaya — see 33.
  2. The author's argument: Mahaprabhu accepted a guru not out of need but so as not to break the order of the sanatana-dharma — initiation within a sampradaya.
  3. Gopala-guru Gosvami — a disciple of Vakreshvara Pandita, an associate of Mahaprabhu; in Puri he served the Deity of Radhakanta at the Gambhira (Radhakanta-matha).
  4. The well-known four shlokas on the maha-mantra attributed to Gopala-guru. "Hara" is Sri Radha, who steals Krishna's mind; "Rama" is Krishna, who delights Radha (Radha-ramana). This explanation is accepted in the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition.
  5. Verses attributed to the Padma-purana and also cited in Baladeva Vidyabhushana's Prameya-ratnavali. Purushottama in Utkala is Jagannatha Puri.
  6. The succession of the Brahma(-Madhva)-sampradaya as in Kavi Karnapura's Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika (21–26) and in Baladeva; Ishvara Puri, Mahaprabhu's guru, is not named in the shloka (cf. 49). Calling Mahaprabhu's line "Nimananda / Nimanandi" (from the name Nimai) is peculiar to the author; cf. 51.
  7. The Vaishnava-vandana of Devakinandana Dasa, a disciple of Purushottama Thakura (an associate of Nityananda).
  8. The author derives the name "Nimanandi" from Mahaprabhu's childhood name, Nimai. "Nimanandi" usually designates the followers of Nimbarka; the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, headed by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, call their sampradaya the Brahma-Madhva-Gaudiya.
  9. Nilambara Chakravarti — Mahaprabhu's grandfather, who cast His horoscope (CC Adi 14). The last word of the line is unclear in the scan.
  10. Vidagdha-madhava 1.2 (CC Adi 1.4).
  11. I.e. the author is a disciple of Ramasharana Chattaraja, son of Krishnadasa Chattaraja, a disciple of Ramacharana Chakravarti, a disciple of Srinivasa.
  12. The author's ten shlokas on his guru, with an eleventh on the fruit of reciting them. The text of the verses is corrupt in places in the edition (especially the tenth); the translation is approximate. The description of the guru's form follows the pattern of the description of Srinivasa (2.11–20).
  13. The Rudra-sampradaya — Vishnusvami; the Vallabhites (Pushti-marga) trace themselves to it: Vallabhacharya and his son Vitthalanatha (cf. 5.15). "Gokula-dvara" is apparently Gokul, the centre of the Vallabhites.
  14. In the Nimbarkite tradition this story is told of Nimbarka (Nimbaditya) himself, the disciple of Narada; the author places Nimbaditya at the end of a long line after Srinivasacharya and others and attaches the story of the sun above the nim tree to him.
  15. Samvat 1753 and shaka 1618 correspond to 1696 CE ("Rama" = 3, "arrow" = 5, "horse" = 7, "moon" = 1, read from right to left; "vasu" = 8, "moon" = 1, "kala" = 16).
